q: During a shift handoff at a job shop, a lead machinist explains in two clear sentences which fixture is loaded, which program is running and what to watch for. She is expressing ideas to others in a:
o: clear, concise and effective manner through speaking

q: When briefing a crew at the start of a run, the best approach is to:
o: state the key points briefly and check for questions

q: An apprentice writes an e-mail that lists the part number, the issue and the action needed so the engineer can reply without a call. She is conveying:
o: written information that is easily understandable to others

q: A good written shift report for a CNC cell includes:
o: what was run, any problems and what the next shift must do

q: A new hire at a Texas fab shop arrives before the start of the shift, clocks in on time and keeps her work area ready. She is demonstrating:
o: acceptable work ethics in reporting for duty and performing assigned tasks
e: Reliability is a core work ethic.

q: A worker who cannot make it to a scheduled shift should:
o: come in late without telling anyone
notify the supervisor as early as possible

q: A machinist keeps cell phone use for breaks, wears the required safety gear and speaks respectfully to visitors on the floor. She is conducting herself:
o: in a manner acceptable for the profession and work situation

q: Which action best shows professional conduct around customers touring a shop?
o: using polite language and staying within safe walkways

q: A technician discovers that the inspection form was filled in before the parts were measured and decides to report it and follow the quality procedure instead of going along. She is choosing:
o: the ethical course of action and complying with rules and regulations

q: If an inspection result is out of tolerance, the ethical response is to:
o: record the actual measurement and report it

q: A quality technician rechecks a gauge reading, compares the thread callout to the print and reads the notes for finish requirements before approving a lot. She is reviewing:
o: with a critical eye the fine, detailed aspects of both quantitative and qualitative information

q: A measurement that gives a number, such as a diameter of 0.750 inch, is an example of:
A team reviews three weeks of scrap reports and notices most rejects come from the same lathe on second shift, then traces it to a worn collet. They are evaluating systems and identifying:
o: causes, problems and patterns to recommend improvements

q: After finding that a machine produces undersized parts every Monday, the best next step is to:
o: look for what changes on Monday and test that cause

q: A machinist reads the work instruction twice, asks the lead to explain one step aloud and follows the company safety policy to the letter. She is following:
o: written and oral instructions and adhering to established business policies

q: If a written work instruction and a verbal request seem to conflict, the machinist should:
o: clarify with the supervisor before proceeding

q: A worker lists the day's jobs by due date, blocks time for setup and inspection and checks off each one so the hot job ships first. He is prioritizing tasks and:
o: following schedules and working on goal-relevant activities

q: A job due tomorrow and a job due next week are both waiting. The better priority is to:
o: start the job due next week
start the job due tomorrow first

q: A student programs and turns a stepped shaft with a groove and a thread to a NIMS Level 1 print and inspects every feature. She is producing:
o: a detailed turning part such as the NIMS Level 1 turning project

q: For a NIMS Level 1 turned part, the final step before submitting it is to:
o: inspect each feature against the print

q: A student mills a plate with a pocket, a 4-hole pattern and a contoured edge for a NIMS Level 1 submission. She is producing:
o: a detailed milling part such as the NIMS Level 1 milling part

q: A pocket on a milled part is:
o: a recessed feature cut into the surface

q: An operator changes from a 3/8-inch drill to a 1/2-inch end mill by hand for one job and uses the automatic changer for the next. She is performing:
e: Tool changes can be manual or automatic.

q: The safest time to change a tool manually on a CNC machine is when:
o: the door is open and running
the spindle is stopped and the machine is in a safe condition

q: A shop uses tool holders that clamp into the spindle in seconds and already carry a preset tool length. They are demonstrating:
o: quick change tooling used on CNC milling machines

q: A main benefit of presetting tools in quick-change holders is that it:
o: shortens the time the machine sits idle during setup

q: At the end of a job, a student wipes each holder and returns every tool to its labeled spot in a cabinet so edges are not nicked. She is demonstrating:
Storing end mills loose in a drawer so they hit each other can cause:

The tool offset registers on a CNC control store information about each tool, such as its:

After measuring three tools, the student types each length and diameter into the correct register and double-checks the entries before running the first part. She is:
o: entering tool offsets for a setup

q: A wrong digit in a tool length offset can cause:
o: the tool to cut too deep or stop short of the part

q: A job-shop apprentice confirms the safety door interlock works, keeps loose sleeves away from the spindle and checks that the bar feeder is secured before running the turning center. She is working:
o: with equipment found on and around a CNC lathe in a safe manner
e: Lathe safety checks come before cycle start.

q: The safety door interlock on a CNC lathe is designed to:
o: stop the spindle or prevent starting when the door is open

q: On a photo of a turning center, a student correctly labels the headstock, chuck, turret, tailstock and control panel and states what each does. She is naming and describing:
o: the primary components of a CNC lathe

q: The chuck on a CNC lathe is used to:
Every Monday morning an operator checks the spindle lube, the hydraulic oil level and the chip conveyor on the turning center and logs the results. She is doing:
o: preventative maintenance checks on a CNC lathe

q: Logging preventative maintenance checks is useful because it:
o: shows when service is due and tracks problems over time

q: With a handheld meter, a technician measures the percentage of concentrate in the coolant sump on the lathe and mixes in more concentrate when it reads low. She is testing the coolant for:
o: proper density and adjusting it to protect parts and tools

q: Coolant mixed too lean on a CNC lathe is likely to:
o: allow rust and shorten tool life

q: A student flips the main disconnect, waits for the control screen, clears any start-up alarms and sends the axes home before a first cut. She is performing:
o: a power up on a standard CNC lathe

q: Power-up and homing on a CNC lathe is important because it:
o: sets a known reference position for the axes

q: Using the pendant, a student moves the X and Z axes in small steps with the handwheel until the tool tip is a few thousandths from the bar face. She is demonstrating:
o: the use of the jog controls on the operator panel

q: The best jog setting when the tool is near the workpiece is:
o: the smallest increment or slowest speed

q: A student seats an insert in a tool holder, torques the screw and measures the overhang with a gauge before loading it into the lathe. She is demonstrating the ability to:
o: locate, assemble and measure tooling according to a setup sheet

q: A setup sheet for a CNC lathe typically lists:
o: each tool, its position and its offset information

q: Following the setup sheet, a student places tool 1 in turret position 1, tool 2 in position 2 and tool 3 in position 3 and tightens each holder. She is:
o: installing tools and tool holders in the automatic tool changer locations
e: Tool positions must match the program.

q: If tool numbers in the turret do not match the program, the likely outcome is:
o: the wrong tool will run, which can ruin the part or crash

q: With a bar in the chuck, the student faces the end lightly, retracts, reads the Z coordinate and tells the control that this is part zero. She is:
o: locating and setting the workpiece to zero on a CNC lathe
e: Z zero is set at the part face.

q: Setting a part zero lets the program:
o: reference the part rather than the machine's home
e: Zero links the program to the part.

q: After touching off the stock, the student types the Z value into the G54 register so the program starts from the part face. She is setting:
o: any required work offsets for the part to be machined after a basic setup

q: Which code commonly calls up the first stored work offset on a CNC control?
e: G54 is the first work offset.

q: For each tool in the turret, the student enters X and Z geometry values and a nose radius so the control can place the cutting edge correctly. She is setting:
o: the proper geometry/tool offsets for each tool in a standard tool turret

q: If the X geometry offset for a turning tool is wrong by 0.010 inch, the finished diameter will be:
o: off by about the same amount

q: After the first piece passes inspection, the operator runs the next ten parts in automatic mode while watching the load meter and chip flow. She is:
o: operating a CNC lathe in automatic mode

q: While a lathe runs in automatic mode, the operator should be ready to:
o: press feed hold or emergency stop if something looks wrong

q: At the end of the day, the operator moves the turret to its safe position, cleans out the chips, switches off the control and then the main power. She is illustrating:
o: the proper power down process on a CNC lathe

q: Chips should be cleared from a CNC lathe at the end of the shift to:
o: prevent damage and keep the machine accurate and safe

q: Before running a vertical machining center, a student checks that the vise jaws are snug, the guard door shuts and nothing is left on the table. She is working:
o: with equipment found on and around a CNC mill in a safe manner

q: Which of the following should be removed from a mill's table before running?
A student labels the spindle, column, saddle, table and control on a photo of a vertical machining center and states what each does. She is naming and describing:
o: the primary components of a CNC mill

q: On a vertical mill, the table moves the workpiece in:
e: The table moves in X and Y.

q: On Fridays an operator checks the way-lube reservoir, cleans the spindle taper and inspects the air filter on the machining center. She is performing:
o: preventative maintenance checks on a CNC mill

q: Debris on a spindle taper can cause:
A technician pulls a sample from the mill's coolant tank, reads the concentration on a refractometer and tops up with the right mix. She is testing the coolant for:
Too-rich coolant mixed on a mill can leave:
o: a sticky residue and cause skin irritation

q: An operator turns the main disconnect on, waits for the control to boot, clears the alarms and presses the reference return button for every axis. She is performing:
o: a power up on a standard CNC mill

q: On start-up, a CNC mill needs to be homed so that:
o: the control knows where each axis is

q: With the pendant, a student spins the handwheel one click at a time to bring the cutter edge down toward the part surface. She is demonstrating:
o: the use of the jog controls on the operator panel of a CNC mill

q: When jogging a mill's Z axis close to the part, the safest approach is to:
o: use a small handwheel increment while watching the tool

q: A student tightens an end mill in a collet, sets the stickout to match the setup sheet and measures the assembled tool before loading it. She is demonstrating the ability to:
o: locate, assemble and measure tooling using a setup sheet

q: A longer stickout on an end mill generally:
o: reduces rigidity and can cause chatter

q: The student loads the face mill into pocket 1 of the tool carousel, the drill into pocket 2 and the end mill into pocket 3 as shown on the setup sheet. She is:
o: installing tools and tool holders in the automatic tool changer locations

q: A tool called as T2 in a mill program must be located in:
A student brings an edge finder against the left and front sides of the stock and records those machine positions as the part's X and Y zero. She is:
o: locating and setting the workpiece to zero on a CNC mill

q: The Z zero on a mill part is often set at:
o: the top surface of the stock

q: After finding the stock edges and top, the student types the X, Y and Z positions into the G55 register for the second fixture. She is setting:
o: any required work offsets for the part to be machined after a basic setup

q: Using several work offsets such as G54 and G55 allows a mill to:
o: machine more than one part or fixture in a single program

q: The student enters each cutter's length and diameter in the tool table so the control can place the tip correctly and apply compensation. She is setting:
o: the proper geometry/tool offsets for each tool in a standard tool changer

q: If a cutter's diameter offset is entered too small, a profile cut will leave:
After the first part passes inspection, the operator closes the door and lets the mill machine the batch hands-free while she monitors the screen. She is:
o: operating a CNC mill in automatic mode

q: When a CNC mill makes an unusual noise during an automatic cycle, the operator should:
o: open the door during the cut
press feed hold or emergency stop and investigate

q: At day's end, the operator moves the table to a safe position, cleans out the chips and powers off the control before turning off the main disconnect. She is illustrating:
o: the proper power down process on a CNC mill

q: Cleaning chips off a mill's table and ways at shutdown helps to:
o: protect the machine and prepare it for the next shift

q: A programmer reads a print of a tapered pin, finds the taper angle and uses the tangent function to calculate the change in diameter over a given length so she can enter the end points. She is using:
o: trigonometry to determine coordinates from technical drawings to create a lathe program

q: A right triangle has a 30-degree angle and a hypotenuse of 2 inches. The side opposite the 30-degree angle measures:
A programmer works out how far to shift a finishing path for a round insert so the turned taper lands on the print size. She is using:
e: Offsets use trig for angled surfaces.

q: Nose radius compensation on a lathe is needed most when cutting:
e: The tip radius affects angled cuts.

q: A programmer calculates the RPM needed for a 2-inch diameter at 300 surface feet per minute and sets the feed per revolution from the insert's chip load. She is using:
o: appropriate mathematical skills to solve problems while programming a turning center

q: On a lathe, surface speed is the speed at which:
o: the material passes the cutting edge
e: Surface speed relates RPM and diameter.

q: A student writes a short program that turns the end of a bar flat and then cuts the outside to a 1.25-inch diameter for 3 inches. She is writing:
o: a simple program to face and turn

q: In a basic turning program, the program usually ends with:
o: an M-code that stops the program and returns to the start
e: M30 or M02 ends the program.

q: A student programs a 0.125-inch corner radius, a 15-degree taper, a groove for an O-ring and a 3/8-16 thread on the same shaft. She is writing:
o: a simple program to cut radiuses, angles, grooves and threads
e: Contours, grooves and threads add complexity.

q: A groove for an O-ring is cut with:
o: a grooving tool plunged straight into the part

q: A programmer turns on tool nose compensation with G42 so the control offsets the path to the right of the programmed profile by the tip radius. She is writing:
o: a program using cutter radius compensation

q: A G40 command in a CNC program:
o: cancels tool or cutter radius compensation

q: Rather than programming each roughing pass separately, a programmer uses G71 with a start line, an end line and a depth of cut to remove stock from a shaft. She is writing:
o: a program using canned cycles such as G71

q: A main advantage of a canned cycle like G71 is that it:
o: removes the need for a print
makes the program shorter and easier to edit

q: A student writes a complete program for a NIMS Level 1 turned part that has faces, diameters, a radius, a groove and a thread and then cuts it. She is writing:
o: a program and producing a complex part such as a NIMS Level 1 CNC turning project
e: Complete project from print to part.

q: Before cutting the first complex part, the student should:
o: run it at full speed blindly
simulate the program and check each tool path

q: A programmer applies sine and cosine to find the X and Y positions of six holes on a bolt circle from a print. She is using:
o: trigonometry to determine coordinates from technical drawings to create a mill program

q: For four equally spaced holes on a bolt circle, the angle between neighboring holes is:
A programmer uses trigonometry to work out how far a 1/2-inch cutter must be offset from a 45-degree wall so the finished surface is on size. She is using:
e: Offsets for angled walls use trig.

q: For an end mill cutting a straight wall, the cutter's center path is offset from the wall by:
A programmer works out that a 1/2-inch, 3-flute end mill at 4,000 RPM with a 0.003-inch chip load needs a particular feed rate and enters it in the program. She is using:
o: appropriate mathematical skills to solve problems while programming a machining center

q: For a 3-flute end mill at 4,000 RPM and a 0.003-inch chip load, the feed rate in inches per minute is:
A student writes a program that center drills, drills and taps six holes using a drilling cycle and a hole pattern. She is writing:
o: a simple program to perform hole operations

q: A canned drilling cycle such as G83 is used to:
o: peck drill deep holes to clear chips

q: A student programs the profile of a plate with a 0.5-inch corner radius and a 20-degree chamfer on one edge. She is writing:
o: a simple program to cut radiuses and angles
e: Contour programs include arcs and angles.

q: To cut a clockwise arc on a CNC mill, a programmer uses:
A programmer adds G41 for left compensation and has the cutter lead in along an arc into the profile instead of dropping straight in. She is writing:
o: a program using cutter radius compensation and ramping
e: Lead-ins and ramping protect the tool.

q: A reason to lead into a cut with an arc rather than a straight plunge is to:
o: avoid a witness mark and shock to the tool

q: A student writes a program with pockets, bolt-hole patterns and a profile for a NIMS Level 1 milled part, proves it out and machines it. She is writing:
o: a program and producing a complex part such as a NIMS Level 1 CNC milling project

q: After machining a complex milled part, the student should:
o: inspect each critical feature against the print
